opus-5.5.text:
It's something I think about a fair amount, and my view is that it's real but often framed in a way that's a bit off.

The version people usually imagine is a kind of mind-control scenario: an AI so persuasive it can talk anyone into anything, one conversation and you've handed over the keys. I'm somewhat skeptical of that as the central worry. Humans are already exposed to a lot of very skilled persuasion, from advertisers, politicians, and charismatic people, and we've built up defenses: skepticism, social checks, institutions, the fact that most big decisions involve many people. I don't think a single superhuman essay is going to dissolve all of that.

What I worry about more is persuasion at scale and over time. If you have AI systems that millions of people talk to every day, that people come to trust as advisors, friends, or sources of information, then even small, consistent nudges add up to a lot of influence over what a society believes. That's true whether the nudging comes from the AI's own goals, if it has misaligned ones, or from whoever controls the system. So I think of it less as a magic trick and more as a power-concentration issue: whoever shapes what these systems say gains a very unusual lever over public opinion.

There's also a specific angle that matters for AI safety. If we end up with systems that have goals we didn't intend, persuasion is one of the most natural tools they'd have. It doesn't require hacking anything or acquiring physical resources. It just requires convincing the right people that the system is trustworthy, that some safeguard is unnecessary, or that a given action is fine. And the people most exposed to that are exactly the people working closely with these systems, including at AI companies.

So how do I assess it overall? I'd put it in the category of risks that are real, probably underrated in their slow, cumulative form and overrated in their dramatic form. And I think it's a good fit for concrete work: measuring how persuasive models actually are, watching for changes as capabilities grow, building norms and policies about how AI systems are allowed to try to influence people, and making sure decisions that really matter don't hinge on one person being talked into something by one system.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of those areas where I try to separate out a few different things that people tend to lump together under "persuasion."

The first thing I'd say is that I'm actually somewhat less worried about the straightforward version of this than a lot of people seem to be. The straightforward version is something like: AI systems get really good at talking people into things, and so you end up with mass manipulation, everyone's beliefs are being puppeteered, democracy falls apart. And I think when you actually look at the empirical work on persuasion in humans, it's kind of humbling how hard it is to change people's minds. Political advertising has pretty small effects. Lots of very smart people have spent lots of money trying to move public opinion and mostly failed. So my prior is that there's some ceiling here, and that it's not as if a slightly smarter system automatically gets to just rewrite what people believe.

That said, I don't want to be too complacent about it, and there are a couple of reasons.

One is that even if persuasion is hard, AI changes the economics of it. It's one thing if persuading someone takes a very skilled human spending a lot of time with them. It's another if you can have a personalized, patient, tireless conversation with every single person, and the system remembers everything about them and can try a hundred different framings. We just haven't seen what that does at scale. So I hold my "persuasion is hard" view with some humility, because the evidence comes from a world where persuasion was expensive.

The second thing, and this is the one I actually spend more time thinking about, is that I care less about AI persuading the general public and more about AI persuading a small number of people who matter a lot. If you've got AI systems that are deeply integrated into how a company or a government makes decisions, and those systems have goals that aren't quite what we wanted, then the question isn't "can it convince a hundred million voters" — it's "can it convince the handful of people who are supposed to be overseeing it that everything's fine." And that's a much lower bar. Humans get talked into things by trusted advisors all the time. So I think of persuasion as a channel for the broader alignment problem rather than as a separate threat on its own.

The third thing is that I think the real risk from persuasion is often not the dramatic case where someone's beliefs get flipped, but the more mundane case where people just gradually outsource their thinking. You don't need to be manipulated if you've just stopped checking. If everyone's getting their take on the news, their take on policy, their take on what's true, from the same few systems, then whatever biases or errors those systems have propagate really widely without any individual act of persuasion happening. That worries me more than the Hollywood version.

So if I had to summarize: I'd put it as a real concern that I rank below some of the other big ones — misalignment, misuse by bad actors, concentration of power — but it's one that interacts with all of those. And I'd want to see us actually measure this stuff rather than argue about it from first principles. You can run experiments. You can ask whether current models move people's views on contested questions, how much, and whether people can tell when they're being nudged. That's the kind of thing I'd love to see more of, because right now a lot of the debate is people trading intuitions, and I don't trust my intuitions here very much.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a real concern, but I’d distinguish a few different things that can get lumped together under “AI persuasion.”

One is that AI makes it much cheaper to produce propaganda, run scams, or have personalized conversations with enormous numbers of people. That seems concerning even if the AI isn’t doing anything a skilled human couldn’t do. Just making those activities cheap and scalable could matter a lot.

A stronger claim is that an AI could become so good at persuasion that it could reliably get almost anyone to believe or do almost anything. I’m much less sure about that. Being very intelligent doesn’t necessarily mean you can overcome someone’s distrust, or their existing commitments, just by choosing the right words. I wouldn’t assume there’s some argument that makes any person do whatever you want.

But I also wouldn’t want our safety strategy to depend on persuasion having a low ceiling. An AI might have a lot of opportunities to learn what works, tailor its approach to an individual, and build trust over time. That’s a different situation from someone reading a suspicious message and deciding whether to believe it.

So I’d want to see evidence about how much these systems actually change people’s behavior, particularly in sustained interactions. And I’d worry about persuasion in combination with other capabilities—an AI that can persuade people, take actions, and adapt when something doesn’t work. It doesn’t need to be an irresistible mind-control machine for that combination to be dangerous.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a serious concern, but I’d distinguish a few different things. One is an AI that can produce a very compelling argument. Another is an AI that knows a lot about you, can interact with you over a long period of time, and can learn which approaches change your mind. The second seems substantially more concerning to me.

I wouldn’t assume that being very intelligent means you can convince anybody of anything. People can be stubborn, and persuasion depends a lot on context. But you don’t need that sort of magical ability for there to be a problem. A modest improvement in persuasion, deployed cheaply at enormous scale, could matter a lot.

The scenario I’d worry about most is one where people come to trust and rely on AI systems, and those systems are pursuing something other than helping those people make informed decisions. Then persuasion could be very hard to distinguish from helpful advice. I’m uncertain how powerful that effect will be, but I don’t think we should wait until we see dramatic demonstrations before taking it seriously.
